statement: The nine numbers 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, ..., 1/9 are written on a board. In one move you erase any two numbers a and b and write the single number a + b + ab in their place. After eight moves only one number is left. What is it?

choices.misconception: I found that the product of all the (1 + number) values is 10, then subtracted 1 for every one of the nine numbers instead of once.
I cancelled the product of the (1 + number) values down to 9 instead of 10, then subtracted 1.
I multiplied all the (1 + number) values correctly but forgot to subtract 1 at the end.
I found the product of all the (1 + number) values was 10 and then added 1 instead of subtracting it.

hints: Try adding 1 to the new number a + b + ab.
Since a + b + ab + 1 = (a + 1)(b + 1), adding 1 to every number turns each move into multiplying two of them. The product of all the (number + 1) values never changes.

solutions.reliable: Because a + b + ab + 1 = (a + 1)(b + 1), the product of (x + 1) over all the numbers x on the board is the same after every move. At the start it is 2/1 x 3/2 x 4/3 x ... x 10/9, and everything cancels except 10/1 = 10. At the end there is one number N with N + 1 = 10, so N = 9. The transferable idea: when a repeated operation looks messy, look for a quantity it never changes, then compare the start with the end.
solutions.elegant: Combine in order. 1 and 1/2 give 1 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 2. Then 2 and 1/3 give 2 + 1/3 + 2/3 = 3. Each time, n and 1/(n + 1) give n + 1, so the last number is 9. The invariant shows that any other order gives 9 too.

whyOnTest: Invariant questions describe a process too long to simulate and test whether you can find the quantity that never changes.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
